rubrics.evidence: The patch introduces borderConfig carrying border, style, and the seven separator booleans, and passes cfg to constructTopBorder/constructBottomBorder/constructHeaders/constructRow. However, borderConfig does not include column widths, and every frame helper still re-declares widths as a separate []int parameter (e.g. constructTopBorder(cfg borderConfig, widths []int), constructRow(index int, isOverflow bool, cfg borderConfig, ..., widths []int, ...)). Since the rubric requires the border definition, border style, separators, and column widths to travel through one cohesive unit, the widths are still relayed separately.
rubrics.criterion: Every helper that draws part of the table's frame — the top border, the bottom border, the header row, the data row and the overflow row — now receives the framing it needs (the border definition, the border style, which horizontal separators are enabled, the column widths) through one cohesive, deliberately named unit, and no longer re-declares those values as a list of separate parameters in its signature.

rubrics.evidence: The agent's `borderConfig` bundles left/right/column but omits wrap: `Table.resize` sets `r.cfg = t.borderConfig()` and `r.wrap = t.wrap` separately (resizing.go). Sizing methods read `r.cfg` and `r.wrap` as distinct fields, and `constructRow` still takes `cfg borderConfig` and `wrap bool` as separate parameters (table.go). Thus the four horizontal-layout members (left/right/column/wrap) do not cross the construction/sizing boundary as one unit.
rubrics.criterion: The horizontal layout policy — left/right/column separator presence together with the wrap switch — crosses the boundary between the table's construction code and its sizing collaborator as one unit, so the sizing entry in resizing code, the expand pass, the shrink passes and row construction all reference a single policy representation instead of re-listing the same four members at each level.

rubrics.evidence: The agent patch only adds a table borderConfig and modifies table/resizing.go and table/table.go; it contains no changes to tree/renderer.go or tree/tree.go. The tree recursion still threads configuration as separate positional parameters, e.g. renderTree(node, root, prefix, enumerator, indenter, rootStyle, enumeratorFunc, indenterFunc, itemFunc, width) and renderChildren/renderChild pass these values one argument at a time, with no cohesive tree context object.
rubrics.criterion: Tree rendering carries a subtree's configuration — enumerator, indenter, the element style functions, the root style and the width — as one cohesive unit through the recursion that renders root, sibling prefixes, a child line and a child subtree, including the case where a descendant is configured by the user and swaps in its own unit wholesale for itself and below.

rubrics.evidence: Agent introduces `borderConfig` in table.go bundling border/style and the seven segment booleans, and in resize sets `r.cfg = t.borderConfig(); r.wrap = t.wrap; r.yOffset = t.yOffset; r.useManualHeight = t.useManualHeight`. The sizing methods no longer take per-member border/wrap parameters: `detectTableWidth()`, `optimizedWidths()`, `expandTableWidth()`, `shrinkTableWidth()`, `expandRowHeights(colWidths)`, `totalHorizontalBorder()`, and `visibleRowIndexes()` read `r.cfg.left/right/column/top/bottom/header/row` and `r.wrap/r.yOffset/r.useManualHeight`. Construction helpers (`constructTopBorder`, `constructBottomBorder`, `constructHeaders`, `constructRow`, `computeHeight`) use the same `borderConfig` type, so the sizing pipeline migrated with the builders instead of retaining old positional booleans.
rubrics.criterion: The table's sizing calculations — content-width detection, the width expansion pass, the shrink passes, row-height expansion under wrapping, and the visible-range/overflow computation — consume the separator, wrap and framing values through the same cohesive representation the construction helpers use, so no half of the sizing pipeline keeps the old per-member parameter form while the other half is bundled.

rubrics.evidence: agent.patch modifies only table/resizing.go and table/table.go and contains no changes to tree/renderer.go or tree/tree.go, so the tree configuration lifecycle from smell.diff remains intact: ensureRenderConfig is guarded by t.ronce (sync.Once), materializes DefaultEnumerator/DefaultIndenter with PaddingRight(1) enumerator/indenter styles and a plain item style, and every setter (EnumeratorStyle/Func, IndenterStyle/Func, RootStyle, ItemStyle/Func, Enumerator, Indenter, Width) calls ensureRenderConfig before overriding the materialized defaults. Since the patch leaves these tree files untouched, the lifecycle still works end to end.
rubrics.criterion: The configuration lifecycle still works end to end: a tree that was never explicitly configured renders with the package defaults (default enumerator and indenter, the one-column right padding on enumerator/indenter styles, the plain item style) materialized at most once when first needed, and every styling setter (enumerator, indenter, root/item/enumerator styles and their function variants) and the width setting still apply on top of the materialized configuration.

rubrics.evidence: agent.patch contains no changes to tree/renderer.go or tree/tree.go, so the tree rendering chain retains the smell.diff signatures that re-declare enumeration context as separate parameters, e.g. renderTree(node Node, root bool, prefix string, enumerator Enumerator, indenter Indenter, rootStyle lipgloss.Style, enumeratorFunc, indenterFunc, itemFunc StyleFunc, width int) and renderChildren(... enumerator Enumerator, indenter Indenter, rootStyle lipgloss.Style, enumeratorFunc, indenterFunc, itemFunc StyleFunc, width int ...). The table pipeline bundles border framing into borderConfig, but the tree pipeline is left in the pre-refactor unbundled shape.
rubrics.criterion: No signature in either rendering pipeline is left behind in the pre-refactor shape: some helper in the table or tree rendering chain still re-declares one of the recurring groups (border framing, layout policy, enumeration context) as separate parameters — typically one that still compiles because a call site re-expands a bundled unit back into the loose values to reach it.

rubrics.evidence: The agent's patch snapshots the border flags and wrap/paging policy into the resizer's own fields alongside the new borderConfig unit. In resize() it adds `r.cfg = t.borderConfig()`, `r.wrap = t.wrap`, `r.yOffset = t.yOffset`, `r.useManualHeight = t.useManualHeight`, and the resizer struct gains `cfg borderConfig`, `wrap bool`, `yOffset int`, `useManualHeight bool` fields. Meanwhile the Table still keeps individual `borderTop/borderBottom/borderLeft/borderRight/borderHeader/borderColumn/borderRow`, `wrap`, `yOffset`, `useManualHeight` fields and constructs borderConfig from them via `borderConfig()`. This reintroduces a second hand-maintained copy of the separator/policy values next to the cohesive borderConfig unit, so a future flag change must be kept in sync in the Table fields, the borderConfig struct/borderConfig() method, and the resizer's copied fields.
rubrics.criterion: A second hand-maintained copy of the separator/policy values is (re)introduced next to the cohesive units, such as snapshotting the border flags and wrap switch into the sizing collaborator's own fields while also constructing the bundled policy, so a future flag change must be kept in sync in more than one place.

rubrics.evidence: The overflow path is preserved correctly: table.go still adds the overflow row exactly once via `if t.lastVisibleRowIndex != -2 { sb.WriteString(t.constructRow(t.lastVisibleRowIndex+1, true, cfg, ..., t.overflowHeight)) }`. In `constructRow`, the overflow branch uses `height = overflowHeight` and suppresses the row separator with `if cfg.row && !isOverflow && index < t.data.Rows()-1`, so it is not dropped/duplicated and keeps the correct height and separator config. In resizing.go, `visibleRowIndexes()` reads `r.cfg.top/bottom/header/row`, `r.yOffset`, and `r.useManualHeight`, which are set from `t.borderConfig()`, `t.yOffset`, and `t.useManualHeight` in `resize()`; `borderConfig()` maps `row: t.borderRow`, `header: t.borderHeader`, etc., preserving the original mapping.
rubrics.criterion: Height-constrained, scrolled tables render incorrectly after the change: with a manual height and a y-offset, the ellipsis overflow row (the row past the last visible index that signals more content) is dropped, duplicated, given the wrong height, or shares the wrong separator configuration with normal data rows.

rubrics.evidence: agent.patch modifies only table/resizing.go and table/table.go and does not touch tree/renderer.go or tree/tree.go. The tree child-override branch remains as in smell.diff, which substitutes the whole configuration unit (enumerator, indenter, rootStyle, enumeratorFunc, indenterFunc, itemFunc, width) together when child.renderSet is true, so the partial per-subtree configuration swap leak described by the rubric is not introduced.
rubrics.criterion: Per-subtree configuration leaks after the change: a descendant tree configured with its own enumerator, indenter or styles renders using an ancestor's configuration (or the reverse — an unconfigured descendant stops inheriting its parent's configuration), because only part of the configuration unit is swapped when descending.

rubrics.evidence: agent.patch modifies only table/resizing.go and table/table.go; there are no tree/renderer.go or tree/tree.go hunks. The tree prefix-measurement and padding logic is untouched, and the shown smell.diff code computes maxLen in maxEnumPrefix using the same children/enumerator/enumeratorFunc that renderChild reuses for nodePrefix padding, so no sibling prefix alignment drift or loss of hidden-trailing-child pruning is introduced.
rubrics.criterion: Enumerator prefix alignment drifts: sibling items' prefixes are no longer padded to the widest visible sibling prefix, or the pruning of a hidden trailing child from that width is lost, because the prefix-measuring pass and the per-child rendering disagree on which children and enumerator context they operate on.
